item.title: 7 Takeaways From a New Poll on the Michigan Senate Race
item.description:
Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for Senate in Michigan, holds a modest lead over the Republican nominee, Mike Rogers, with six weeks until Election Day, according to a new poll from The New York Times and Siena University.

Dr. El-Sayed has a five-point edge over Mr. Rogers, 49 percent to 44 percent, the survey found, and is viewed more favorably by voters. The race in Michigan, a perennial swing state, is one of a handful of competitive contests that could decide control of the Senate.

Mr. Rogers, a former congressman backed by President Trump, has sought to distance himself from the increasingly unpopular president in recent days, including by calling for an end to the war with Iran. Dr. El-Sayed, a progressive, is working to heal wounds from a bitter primary.

Here are seven takeaways from the poll.

Forty-six percent of Michigan voters said Dr. El-Sayed, a former public health official, had good character, while 39 percent said the same of Mr. Rogers, a former congressman. Dr. El-Sayed also held an edge in the number of people who view him favorably, 47 percent to 39 percent. But a significant number of voters also view Dr. El-Sayed very unfavorably, 35 percent for Dr. El-Sayed, compared with 27 percent for Mr. Rogers.

Mr. Rogers, 63, led Dr. El-Sayed, 41, by nine points with voters ages 45 and up, a bloc that makes up two-thirds of the likely electorate. Among voters 44 or younger, Mr. Rogers trails Dr. El-Sayed by 39 percentage voters, the poll found.

Mr. Rogers has been trying to win independents and peel off Democrats by portraying Dr. El-Sayed as an extremist. The results suggested he has met with mixed results: Dr. El-Sayed held a one-point lead with independents. And just 3 percent of Democrats said they planned to back Mr. Rogers, which was about equal to the share of Republicans who said they planned to support Dr. El-Sayed. Still, more voters in the poll said Dr. El-Sayed was more extreme (50 percent) than said Mr. Rogers was more extreme (36 percent).

Dr. El-Sayed has called for strong A.I. guardrails (including a pause on A.I. development), and Mr. Rogers split with Mr. Trump, who has largely dismissed any risks, by saying he would make A.I. regulation a top priority if elected. Dr. El-Sayed held an 11-point edge over Mr. Rogers in a poll question about who would be better on A.I. data centers.

The streamer, Hasan Piker, campaigned with Dr. El-Sayed in the Democratic primary. A fierce critic of Israel who has a history of provocative commentary, Mr. Piker is viewed very unfavorably by 29 percent of Michigan voters, somewhat unfavorably by 5 percent, according to the poll. Only six percent viewed him very or somewhat favorably, according to the poll. Still, despite Mr. Rogers’s efforts to push Mr. Piker to the center of the campaign, most Michigan voters said they had not heard of him.

Dr. El-Sayed’s primary victory over Representative Haley Stevens featured sharp insults and barbed disagreements about Israel. But 62 percent of Democrats and Democratic-leaning voters in Michigan said the vigorous debate during the primary made the party stronger, according to the poll, compared with 27 percent who said it weakened Democrats by exposing divisions.

Mr. Rogers served for more than a decade in Congress, but voters are not sure he would be a better senator than Dr. El-Sayed, who has never been a lawmaker. Forty-seven percent of voters said Dr. El-Sayed would be more effective in Congress, while 43 percent said Mr. Rogers would be better, the poll found.

item.title: Iranian American Group Files Suit Alleging Iran War Is Unconstitutional
item.description:
An Iranian American organization filed a federal lawsuit on Thursday arguing that the Trump administration usurped Congress’s power to declare war through its roughly seven months of military operations in Iran.

The lawsuit, filed in Federal District Court in Washington, came two days after President Trump escalated threats against Iran in front of the United Nations, saying that he was considering whether to “annihilate” the country or strike a deal. The advocacy arm of the National Iranian American Council, which brought the lawsuit, argued the war had harmed many of its members, who have relatives in Iran who have been killed, injured or had their livelihoods destroyed because of the Trump administration’s bombing and economic pressure.

The lawsuit asks a federal judge to declare the war with Iran unconstitutional. The group wrote that the founders intended to leave “the question of war or peace” to Congress and not the president.

“That was the understanding of every participant in drafting, debating and ratifying the Constitution, and it remains the correct understanding today,” they wrote.

Congress enacted legislation in 1973 requiring the president to observe certain limits when ordering military operations, but courts have tended to defer to the president’s authority to conduct war as commander in chief of the armed forces.

In 1974, the Supreme Court declined to overturn a lower court’s decision allowing President Richard M. Nixon to carry out bombing campaigns in Cambodia during the Vietnam War without authorization from Congress. The lower court found then that the legality of the bombings was a political question not reviewable by the courts.

The lawsuit on Thursday followed several bipartisan efforts by lawmakers this year to pass a measure to pressure the president into ending the war or seeking congressional approval. But the measures, called war powers resolutions, do not carry the force of law and were repeatedly brushed aside by the White House.

item.title: Appeals Court Rejects Finding That Texas Woman on Death Row Is Innocent
item.description:
The Texas Court of Criminal Appeals rejected a lower court’s finding on Thursday that a woman on death row was innocent in the 2007 death of her 2-year-old daughter.

The woman, Melissa Lucio, 58, was sentenced to death in 2008 after being convicted of capital murder in the death of her daughter, Mariah Alvarez. Ms. Lucio’s lawyers have long maintained that Mariah had died from complications after accidentally falling down a flight of stairs.

The 5-4 decision from the Texas Court of Criminal Appeals, the state’s highest criminal court, was the latest turn in a lengthy legal case that drew attention from state lawmakers, faith groups and other organizations.

Ms. Lucio was days away from execution in April 2022 when the Texas Court of Criminal Appeals stopped it and ordered a closer look at her case. The court asked Judge Arturo Nelson, who has presided over the trial, to review the evidence and report back.

In April 2024, Luis Saenz, the Cameron County district attorney, said his predecessor had withheld evidence that would have benefited Ms. Lucio. Later that year, Judge Nelson declared that Ms. Lucio was “actually innocent; she did not kill her daughter.”

On Thursday, the Texas Court of Criminal Appeals said that it rejected the lower court’s findings, which relied too heavily on Ms. Lucio’s interpretations of events.

“After careful review, we conclude that the record before us does not support a grant of habeas relief on any of applicant’s remanded allegations,” the court said in an unsigned opinion.

Of the nine judges, three dissented and filed opinions, while another judge dissented without filing an opinion. In one dissenting opinion, Judge Lee Finley said that Judge Nelson was “in a better position than this court to make the determination of whether the state’s concession of error is credible.”

Vanessa Potkin, a lawyer for Ms. Lucio, said in a statement that she planned to ask a federal court to stop the execution.

“Between Judge Nelson’s detailed findings of innocence, and District Attorney Saenz’s concession of error, we are confident that the courts will clear Melissa Lucio and allow her to return home to her children and grandchildren,” Ms. Potkin said. “Justice will be done.”

When Mariah died in 2007, Ms. Lucio was pregnant with twins and had 12 children. Ms. Lucio has long maintained her innocence.

According to the Texas Department of Criminal Justice, paramedics were called to Ms. Lucio’s home in Cameron County on Feb. 17, 2007, when they found an unresponsive 2-year-old child.

Ms. Lucio’s lawyers said that Mariah had fallen down a flight of stairs, and two days later, she did not wake up from a nap. An autopsy report said that the cause of death was blunt force trauma to the head.

item.title: An Idaho Cold Case Revisits the Unsolved Tylenol Killings in 1982
item.description:
On Dec. 4, 1982, a man used sodium cyanide to kill himself in Sacred Heart Catholic Church in Boise, Idaho. For the next four decades, he was known only as the “Unknown Wanderer” until investigators announced on Wednesday that they had identified him as Dr. Mathew Betkouski, an organic chemist.

When the Ada County Sheriff’s Office said its investigators had solved the cold case, it also announced the discovery of a possible link to another mystery, one that had gripped the nation that year when Extra-Strength Tylenol capsules were lethally tainted with potassium cyanide.

Seven people in the Chicago area died after ingesting the tainted pills, and the case prompted makers of over-the-counter drugs to introduce new safety features.

“Identifying the Unknown Wanderer opened an unexpected door,” the sheriff’s office said in a statement.

Tim Cooper, a detective with the Ada County Sheriff’s Office, added, “We’re hoping that getting his story out generates new leads, not just for this case, but for others we may not even know about yet.”

The sheriff’s office said it was withholding some of what it called supporting evidence for a possible connection between Dr. Betkouski and the Tylenol killings, saying a full account would be revealed in the Oct. 9 release of “Unmasking the Tylenol Killer,” a documentary it had worked on with the television series “Unsolved Mysteries.”

While the authorities in Idaho are not calling Dr. Betkouski a suspect in the Tylenol case, they said they had shared their findings with the Chicago Police Department, which confirmed it has been in contact to determine whether there is a connection.

The Chicago police said in a statement on Thursday that the Tylenol investigation “remains an open cold case” and that it was inviting tips from the public.

The Arlington Heights Police Department in Illinois said in a statement on Thursday that it had also received information about the findings from the Idaho investigators. It said it was working with the F.B.I. and other agencies “to identify the individual or individuals responsible for the 1982 Tylenol murders.”

The Tylenol poisonings date to September 1982, when a 12-year-old girl, Mary Kellerman, died after swallowing a capsule to fend off a cold. Six more people in the Chicago area died after taking Tylenol.

The Food and Drug Administration warned consumers nationwide to stop using Extra-Strength Tylenol. The manufacturer, the McNeil Consumer Products division of Johnson & Johnson, recalled specific lots of the capsules, and offered a $100,000 reward for information leading to the arrest and conviction of the “person or persons responsible for the murders.”

Some states banned sales. Stores removed the capsules from their shelves.

“You’re dealing here with an absolutely monstrous crime,” Bob Fletcher, a spokesman for the Illinois Department of Law Enforcement, told The New York Times in 1982. “Whether it’s a psychotic individual, whether it’s targeted at one particular person, whether it’s a perverted juvenile prank — there’s simply a universe of possibilities in the case.”

Several men were questioned, but the leads went nowhere. One man, James W. Lewis, a tax consultant, sent a letter to the manufacturer saying he would “stop the killing” in exchange for a million dollars. He was arrested and spent 12 years in federal prison for extortion.

As the killings remained unsolved, investigators continued to scrutinize Mr. Lewis. In 2009, F.B.I. agents executed a search warrant at his residence in Cambridge, Mass. In 2022, investigators traveled from Illinois to speak with him, the CBS affiliate in Chicago reported at the time.

Mr. Lewis was never charged in the murders, and he denied any involvement. He died in 2023.

Meanwhile, Detective Cooper reopened the “Unknown Wanderer” cold case in 2019. The body found in the church in Boise had in his possession 19 $100 bills, about 30 keys and a typed note signed William L Toomey, a name that proved fake, Sheriff Matt Clifford said at a news conference on Wednesday. The county coroner determined that the man had died of cyanide poisoning, the sheriff’s statement said.

An engraving on a key led investigators to a street, Mills Court, in Jacksonville, Fla., where records showed a property owner who had disappeared in 1982 and was declared dead in 1989 in absentia. A DNA sample from a family member yielded his name, Detective Cooper said.

His story slowly emerged in the investigation. He grew up in Los Angeles, and in 1974 he had a traumatic brain injury after a fall, Detective Cooper said, adding that “his mental illness throughout his life was complicated.”

Investigators spoke to people who knew him, leading to what the sheriff’s office described as his “possible connection” to the Tylenol murders. He had worked in drugstores in Florida, had a volatile nature and a fascination with explosives, the investigation showed. Colleagues said he had discussed the idea of a “perfect crime” with cyanide as an undetected killer.

During the investigation, Detective Cooper discovered that Dr. Betkouski was hired by Lockheed in 1979 and worked on a NASA project at the White Sands Test Facility in New Mexico, where a former colleague said he had spoken about how “poison could be introduced into over-the-counter capsules if a person wished to do so.”

His employment there ended in March 1982, after he created a “disturbance” while trying to obtain capsules from a pharmacy in the Las Cruces area for what he called an “experiment,” Detective Cooper said at the news conference.

A map of Chicago and a small bottle of sodium cyanide were found among his belongings, Detective Cooper said, noting that a different type, potassium cyanide, was used in the Tylenol poisonings. Photographs showed he had visited Chicago, but investigators “cannot place him” there at the time of the murders in 1982, he said.

“Our goal today is to generate new leads,” he said. “We’re especially interested in Dr. Betkouski’s movements between Oct. 15 and Dec. 4, 1982.”

item.title: Hiker Is Found Dead on Washington Trail After Fall
item.description:
A man died after plummeting several hundred feet during a mountain hike in Washington last week, local authorities said, days after another hiker died on the same mountain.

Gary Idleburg, 66, of Olympia, Wash., was hiking on a zigzagging switchback trail on Sauk Mountain on Saturday when other hikers observed him falling 800 to 1,000 feet off the edge of the trail, the Skagit County Sheriff’s Office said in a statement released earlier this week.

“Emergency personnel immediately began lifesaving efforts; however, Mr. Idleburg was pronounced deceased at the scene,” the Sheriff’s Office said.

Sauk Mountain, which is about 100 miles north of Seattle, reaches a peak of about 5,500 feet and has a popular hiking trail filled with switchbacks.

Mr. Idleburg’s death came two days after another hiker on the mountain, Peter Kalapaca, 78, was reported missing, the Sheriff’s Office said in a separate statement this week.

Mr. Kalapaca was last seen about 12:30 p.m. on Sept. 17 near the top of the Sauk Mountain Trail. During search efforts the following day and evening, a helicopter crew found Mr. Kalapaca “in steep terrain that was inaccessible” to ground search and rescue teams, the authorities said.

“Sadly, he was not moving and was deceased when found,” the Sheriff’s Office said. The statement did not describe a cause of death. The Sheriff’s Office did not immediately respond to a request for more details on Thursday.

The Sauk Mountain Trail was temporarily closed during the recovery efforts but has since reopened.

Mr. Kalapaca’s son, Andy, thanked emergency crews for their efforts in a post on Facebook.

“We are fortunate he didn’t suffer and that his last steps were doing something he very much enjoyed rather than a hospice bed,” Andy Kalapaca wrote.

“He went doing what he loved,” he said in a separate post with photos of his father.

The Sauk Mountain trail is a 4.2-mile round-trip, according to the Washington Trails Association.

The trail group described it as “steep and narrow, and in some places eroded from hikers cutting the switchbacks.”

item.title: Who Is the Trump-Appointed Judge Who Blocked the White House Media Ban?
item.description:
On Thursday, Judge Timothy J. Kelly ordered the Trump administration to restore White House access to journalists from CNN, MS NOW and Politico.

In his ruling, he found that barring the news outlets without due process likely amounted to “constitutional harm” that had an impact on the public, as well, “given the importance of the free press.”

Thursday’s ruling made Judge Kelly the latest jurist appointed to the federal bench by President Trump during his first term who has issued a high-profile ruling blocking one of Mr. Trump’s second-term policies.

It was not the first time that Judge Kelly had signaled his independence from Mr. Trump’s preferences. In a similar case from 2018, when Judge Kelly had been on the bench for a little more than a year, he ordered the administration to restore press credentials to Jim Acosta, then CNN’s chief White House correspondent.

Earlier this year, he also called the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol “a perilous event” that jeopardized “the peaceful transfer of power from one president to the next.” He reluctantly dismissed a criminal case against five far-right extremists who had all been convicted of charges stemming from the attack, only to have their sentences pardoned or commuted by Mr. Trump. In that ruling, Judge Kelly questioned whether Mr. Trump’s views about prosecuting Jan. 6 rioters were “based on fact or fiction.”

In 2017, when Judge Kelly was appointed by Mr. Trump to the Federal District Court for the District of Columbia, he already had a record of public service. He had served for a decade in the Justice Department under both Democratic and Republican presidents. As a federal prosecutor, he helped assemble a criminal case against Jeffrey A. Sterling, a former C.I.A. officer convicted in 2015 of espionage on charges that he told a reporter for The New York Times about a secret effort to disrupt Iran’s nuclear program.

He also had strong conservative credentials. He clerked in the Eastern District of Pennsylvania for a judge appointed by President George H.W. Bush. He joined the Federalist Society, a conservative legal group, in 2009 and, according to written testimony he submitted to the Senate, has attended at least four of its annual conventions.

Beginning in 2013, Judge Kelly worked as counsel to Senator Charles E. Grassley, Republican of Iowa, who went on to become chairman of the Senate Judiciary Committee, including when Judge Kelly was confirmed by a 94-to-2 vote. At Judge Kelly’s confirmation hearing, Mr. Grassley called him a “very talented attorney,” praising his “vast legal experience” and “thoughtful approach.”

When asked by a Democratic senator whether he agreed with Mr. Trump’s false claim that millions of people voted illegally in the 2016 presidential election, Judge Kelly declined to answer, citing rules that restrict judges from engaging in “political activity.”

A longtime resident of Washington, Judge Kelly graduated from Georgetown University Law Center before working for Arnold and Porter, a storied Beltway law firm. According to his official court biography, he spent several months of his time there on loan to Legal Aid Society, where he represented low-income Washington residents in matters like landlord-tenant and family disputes.

In 2003, he wrote a letter to the editor of Newsweek reminding readers that $100 million in cash reported to have been found with two sons of Saddam Hussein, the deposed Iraqi dictator, was “the property of the Iraqi people, from whom it was stolen.”

Mr. Trump has repeatedly expressed anger when his picks for federal judgeships and Supreme Court seats at times rule against him. Other trial-court judges chosen by Mr. Trump have blocked his efforts to send the National Guard into Portland, Ore., constrain legal assistance for detained immigrants and summarily deport Venezuelans using an obscure wartime law.

But in at least one instance, in 2017, Judge Kelly issued a major decision supporting Mr. Trump’s policies, when he ruled that Mr. Trump’s pick to lead the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau as acting director could remain in place. The bureau’s deputy director, a career civil servant, had sued, claiming that she had the legal right to lead the agency.

The order restoring White House access to CNN, MS NOW and Politico is temporary and expires after 14 days. Judge Kelly could choose to issue a more lasting ruling, which the government could then appeal.

item.title: ‘Love Me’ Ad Promotes Trump With Public Money Ahead of the Midterms
item.description:
A new ad flashes images of President Trump set to a striking soundtrack: A song titled “Love Me.” Even more striking may be the disclaimer: “Paid for by the U.S. government.”

The commercial debuted this week on right-wing news outlets, according to the media tracking service AdImpact. Mr. Trump has urged Republicans to vote in the November midterms as if he were on the ballot, trying to draw voters who typically turn out only for presidential elections to the polls. He asked Republicans at a midterm convention in Dallas this month to join him in a loyalty oath to himself.

“America will never be a communist country,” Mr. Trump says in the short spot, which aired Wednesday on Fox News in at least some cable television markets, including Miami. The ad, which also trumpets Trump policies, appears to have aired on the right-wing outlet Newsmax as well.

The White House said in a statement on Thursday afternoon that the ads, which do not tell viewers to vote or take any other action, were “public service announcements.”

“The ad is educational and unapologetically patriotic,” the statement said.

A shorter version of the video was posted to the White House’s official YouTube site 11 days ago.

Senator Maggie Hassan, Democrat of New Hampshire, sent a letter earlier Thursday demanding that the White House chief of staff, Susie Wiles, divulge who produced the commercial.

“The advertisement raises deep concerns about the Trump Administration’s use of taxpayer dollars and its compliance with federal laws that prohibit the use of appropriated funds for the promotion of a political party or candidate,” Ms. Hassan wrote in the letter addressed to Ms. Wiles, which was provided to The New York Times.

Hassan, Democrat of New Hampshire, sent a letter demanding that the White House chief of staff, Susie Wiles, divulge who produced a commercial urging Republicans to vote.

Representative Jamie Raskin of Maryland, the top Democrat on the House Judiciary Committee, said that if the White House used government dollars to pay for the ad, it could constitute a violation of federal law. “It is blatantly unethical,” he wrote on X.

Kristi Noem, Mr. Trump’s former homeland security secretary, was fired in March after members of Congress scrutinized a taxpayer-funded ad campaign related to immigration enforcement actions that cost more than $220 million.

Presidents are exempt from the Hatch Act, which restricts partisan political activities for most other executive branch employees. Still, the ad could violate government restrictions against using taxpayer dollars for propaganda, said Norm Eisen, a former White House special counsel for ethics and government reform.

“Congress has established governmentwide restrictions on the use of appropriated funds for publicity or propaganda through annual appropriations bills,” said Mr. Eisen, who has sued the Trump administration on several fronts as co-founder of Democracy Defenders Action. “This commercial is a shocking transgression of those legal provisions.”

In his second term, Mr. Trump has been emboldened to push the legal limits of the presidency, in part because of the Supreme Court ruling that presidents enjoy broad criminal immunity for official acts taken while in office.

The president’s high-powered super PAC, MAGA Inc., has been funding other ads for political campaigns across the country.

The last line in the new ad appears to be delivered by Dana White, the president and chief executive of the Ultimate Fighting Championship. It proclaims that Mr. Trump is “the toughest, most resilient person that I’ve ever met, and nothing was going to stop him from fighting so hard for the country he loves.”

Mr. White appears to have said that at least once, at a Trump rally last year the day before the president’s inauguration.

In a statement, JMSN, the R&B artist who wrote and recorded “Love Me,” said he “did not authorize the use” of the song.

“I am looking for a lawyer now in order to see what our options are and how to proceed,” the emailed statement said. “I have never been in this situation before, so need help in navigating something of this magnitude.”

Shane Goldmacher contributed reporting. Kitty Bennett contributed research.

item.title: Senate Defeats Bid to Direct Trump to End Iran War or Seek Approval
item.description:
The Senate on Thursday narrowly rejected an effort to direct President Trump to end the war in Iran unless he wins authorization for it, defeating a measure aimed at rebuking his handling of a conflict he has continued to wage despite repeated votes by Congress to halt it.

The resolution, which passed the House over the summer, failed 50 to 49, with four Republicans — Senators Susan Collins of Maine, Rand Paul of Kentucky, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska and Thom Tillis of North Carolina — joining Democrats in support. Senator John Fetterman of Pennsylvania was the lone Democrat to oppose the measure.

Mr. Tillis was the newest Republican to break with his party over the war, joining a small bloc that has challenged Mr. Trump’s authority to continue directing the conflict without congressional approval.

But Senator Bill Cassidy, the Louisiana Republican who had previously voted with G.O.P. defectors to curtail Mr. Trump’s war powers, switched his position and sided with the majority of his party on Thursday, leaving the resolution short of the support to pass.

It was the 20th vote on such a resolution since the war began on Feb. 28.

Since the conflict began on Feb. 28, Congress has collectively held 20 Iran war powers votes, six in the House and 14 in the Senate.

That measure could still come before the Senate, giving lawmakers opposed to the war another opportunity to send an identical resolution through both chambers of Congress.

Such a measure would not have the force of law, but would amount to a political rebuke. A growing number of Republicans in both chambers have broken with the president on the conflict as they battle to maintain control of Congress in November and win over constituents feeling the impacts of the war.

Again and again, Democrats have forced votes seeking to restrict Mr. Trump’s ability to carry out the war and to compel him to seek authorization from Congress. And again and again, the president has brushed aside those objections, continuing military operations while Congress debates resolutions that have done nothing to alter their course.

The last time both chambers passed a resolution directing him to end the war, in June, he arrived on Capitol Hill and berated Republicans who supported it, demanding that they reverse their votes. Still, G.O.P. lawmakers have slowly grown more outspoken about the impacts of the war and more willing to vote to challenge the president’s handling of it.

The rebukes have grown more bipartisan and, at times, more emphatic even as their practical consequences have remained negligible.

But the war powers votes have also demonstrated the limits of their strategy. The administration has maintained that the president has sufficient constitutional authority to conduct military operations, and even measures that have cleared Congress have failed to meaningfully constrain him.

item.title: In Alaska, Rowdy Members of Congress Are a Tradition
item.description:
One threatened a fellow congressman at knife point in a dispute over pet spending projects.

Another routinely wore an Incredible Hulk tie to the Capitol in a proud acknowledgment of his foul temper when he wasn’t getting his way.

Revelations about the conduct of former Representative Mary Peltola, a Democrat, toward her staff — including angry outbursts and the use of slurs — drew criticism on Thursday from Republicans who suggested they showed her unfitness for the Senate seat she is seeking.

But it was not clear whether Alaskans, who for decades have elected abrasive, bellicose and occasionally violent individuals to represent them in Congress, would find it disqualifying.

Alaska’s representatives on Capitol Hill have long brought a special brand of coarseness to Washington, part of a frontier mentality and a rough-and-tumble political tradition that comes with a bare-knuckled approach to securing federal resources for their remote state. They often seem to operate with a chip on their shoulder, arguing that their state’s distance leads to its getting short shrift.

“In Alaska, abrasiveness can sometimes read as political charisma, or sometimes even as authenticity, given that Alaska has a political culture that rewards independence,” said Alexander Hirsch, a political science professor at the University of Alaska Fairbanks. “What sometimes reads like irreverence in Washington, D.C., can simultaneously signal to Alaskan voters something that’s really politically attractive.”

Here is a look at a few of the state’s more aggressive characters.

Serving in the Senate for 40 years, Senator Ted Stevens was known as a fierce and often hot-tempered advocate for Alaska. As a member and then chairman of the powerful Appropriations Committee, he funneled billions to his state, including to create the Trans-Alaska Pipeline, which made the state rich. Republicans made Mr. Stevens their second-highest ranking official in the Senate in 1977, a position he held for eight years.

An Army pilot during World War II, Mr. Stevens moved to Alaska in 1953 to practice law and soon afterward became the federal prosecutor there. He used to recount how he accompanied police on raids, gun strapped to his hip. In 1956, he went to Washington to work in the Interior Department on Alaska statehood, helping to bring Alaska into the union and then becoming a ferocious champion of it. He was named Alaskan of the Century in 2000 and a statue of him greets visitors at the Anchorage airport he showered with federal money and which is now named for him.

He was briefly convicted of concealing more than $250,000 in gifts by a federal jury in the District of Columbia in 2008, about a week before he lost a Senate re-election bid. About six months later, a judge threw out the conviction. He died in a plane crash in 2010, at 86, after surviving a serious crash in the 1970s.

When he faced a tough Senate debate, Mr. Stevens wore a tie featuring the image of the Incredible Hulk, the comic book superhero.

“I’m a mean, miserable S.O.B.,” he proclaimed in 1977 as he took over as chairman of the appropriations panel.

Decades later, Mr. Stevens once grabbed a reporter by the lapels in a Capitol hallway and urged him to help vanquish environmental activists who were thwarting his efforts to open a nature preserve to energy development. (The reporter did not.)

Angry that his daughters were not allowed to play Little League Baseball, Mr. Stevens became a fiery proponent of Title IX, guaranteeing gender equity in sports.

His temper was voted the “hottest” on Capitol Hill in a 2006 poll of congressional staff members by Washingtonian magazine.

Mr. Stevens did not argue with the characterization, instead boasting of how he used his hotheadedness to help his state.

“I didn’t lose my temper,” he once said. “I know right where it is.”

Gruff and irascible, Representative Don Young, who survived occasional allegations of shady ethics in his 49 years in the House, was a staunch opponent of environmental causes and a tough defender of Alaska’s oil, mineral and logging industries. He used his powerful leadership positions on two committees to fund highways, bridges, pipelines and many other projects. He passed away in 2022, at 88, while traveling home to Alaska.

Mr. Young moved to Alaska soon after it became a state and tried his hand at fishing, trapping and panning for gold. He was inspired, he said, by “The Call of the Wild,” the 1903 novel by Jack London about a sled dog in Alaska.

In Congress, he cultivated the image of a rugged frontiersman, and at times was crude in public. In a 1994 House debate on the right of Native Alaskans to sell sex organs of endangered animals as aphrodisiacs, he waved an 18-inch walrus penile bone at the face of the fish and wildlife commissioner.

In a radio interview in 2013, he referred to Latino migrant workers with an ethnic slur. In 2014, he forcefully grabbed a congressional staffer’s arm. In 2019, he shoved and cursed at a reporter. And in 2017, the former House speaker John Boehner of Ohio told Politico that Mr. Young had once pinned him against a wall in the Capitol and held a 10-inch knife to his throat, a story the Alaskan conceded at the time was “mostly true.”

His lapses rarely hurt him at the polls. He was elected to 25 consecutive terms, usually facing moderate to light opposition and winning more than 70 percent of the vote five times.

The former senator and governor was much less combative than the other two Alaskans and was overshadowed by Mr. Stevens in some ways. But he was known to be gruff and impatient in his pursuit of federal aid for the state. He left the Senate in 2002 when he was elected governor and he appointed his daughter, Lisa, a state lawmaker, to his seat in what many criticized as a blatant act of nepotism.

Ms. Murkowski went on to become a popular figure who used her positions on key committees to funnel federal money to Alaska and push for more oil drilling. She also had a thick skin, winning re-election in a write-in campaign in 2010 after losing the Republican primary to a Tea Party-affiliated candidate.

Ms. Murkowski, who remains in the Senate, is now known for cultivating an independent streak and breaking with her party on big issues, drawing the wrath of President Trump, whom she voted to convict at his 2021 impeachment trial.

In an Oval Office showdown in 2017, she told Mr. Trump her loyalty was to her state, not her political affiliation.

“With all due respect, Mr. President, I didn’t come here to represent the Republican Party,” she told him then, according to some of those present. “I am representing my constituents and the state of Alaska.”

item.title: Trump Administration Asks Supreme Court to Allow Deportations to Third Countries
item.description:
The Trump administration asked the Supreme Court on Thursday to allow it to continue its program to deport immigrants to countries other than their own.

Administration lawyers filed an emergency application to the justices after a lower federal court on Wednesday upheld a block on the government’s program, finding that people could not be deported without being given a chance to contest their cases.

In the emergency application, Solicitor General D. John Sauer urged the court to allow the administration to continue the deportations, calling the effort “an essential tool to remove certain aliens, including some of the worst criminal aliens.”

Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson, who handles emergency applications from the appeals court that blocked the program, asked the challengers to respond by Monday at 4 p.m.

The third-country deportations have been criticized because the Trump administration has sent immigrants to countries with histories of human rights abuses. Reporting by The New York Times has shown that foreign detainees in the African country of Equatorial Guinea were hooded, bound and beaten by police in a hotel for U.S. deportees from other countries.

But Mr. Sauer argued that the court intervention halting the program had been “unexpected” and had “created substantial logistical problems with ongoing removal operations.” He said the administration had been forced to cancel deportation flights, which had been costly and could lead to diplomatic entanglements — not to mention making it difficult to deport people who he said were “dangerous criminals.”

The emergency application is the latest in a flurry of court actions about the controversial policy, which the Trump administration has used to swiftly deport immigrants, avoiding rules that bar certain people from being returned to their home countries, particularly those who fear persecution or torture.

Earlier this week, James Percival, the top lawyer at the Department of Homeland Security, said on social media that more than 25,000 people had been deported under the program.

The block on the policy by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the First Circuit had sent Trump administration officials scrambling, according to reporting by The Times.

Immediately after the ruling, officials removed immigrants from flights bound to several third countries, including Costa Rica, Honduras and the Central African Republic.

In the emergency filing to the justices, Mr. Sauer told the court that the block by the appeals court had led the Department of Homeland Security to cancel a flight to three separate countries carrying 70 immigrants. He asserted that the cancellation had “required a new round of diplomatic engagement with each of the three countries.”
